text.p: LME aluminium slipped to the softest levels in a month on Tuesday afternoon, dragging other base metals with it, as a correction extended lower.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau index was 0.16 points higher at 237.46.
On the LME, copper headed towards the $2,200 mark, lead extended Monday's losses and notched up fresh 15-1/2 month lows, but zinc was resilient.
"Many of the metals seem to be in a correction phase after having seen some very good run-ups," said analyst Martin Squires at Rudolf Wolff.

Fund selling fed weakness in aluminium after prices on Monday broke out of a $1,600-$1,650 range seen for weeks. Prices touched a low of $1,534, the weakest since January 2, but bounced to end the kerb at $1,547, a $38 loss.

Copper also eased, but a less-than-expected stocks build of 2,650 tonnes and the backwardation helped prop up the market. Three month prices ended at their low of $2,212, down $19 on the day and forming a bearish outside day. A test of the $2,200 level was likely in the near term, analysts said.
Lead etched out a fresh 15-1/2 month low of $634, equalling the nadir on October 18, 1995. But it rebounded slightly to finish the kerb at $644, a loss of $13 from Monday.

Nickel settled at its low of $7,730, down $105 on the day and off recent highs near $8,000. But Tuesday's low was above Monday's weakest level of $7,690. A correction had been expected, since the market's blistering rise had pushed it into overbought territory and it needed to let off some steam, analysts said.
Zinc and tin bucked the trend, ignoring the weakness in the other metals to end $1 higher at $1,176 and unchanged at $5,920, respectively.

CBOT wheat futures rallied late in trading on delays in shipping Canadian wheat which triggered ideas some business may be shifted to the United States, traders said. Transportation problems in Canada include delays in shipments of spring wheat to Asian customers and there also was talk of delays of up to four to six weeks in rail transportation of oats into the U.S., trade sources said. At 1312 CST, wheat was 4-3/4 to 7-1/2 cents per bushel higher, with March up 7-1/2 at $3.60. Oats were 1-1/2 to nine cents per bushel higher, with March up nine at $1.76-1/2.

New York precious metals futures remained lower midday Tuesday, led by further weakness in gold. "The weakness in the complex is being led by gold," Rosko Futures president and COMEX floor trader, John Rosko, said. "March silver is only weak because of some rolling of long positions forward," he said.

COMEX April gold was down $2.60 an ounce at $340.50 midday, but was still holding above the contract low at $339.40 seen last Friday, analysts noted. In the bullion market, spot gold was quoted $338.50/00 midday, compared to the London Tuesday afternoon fix at $339.40, and the New York close Monday around $340.85/35.
CSCE world sugar futures pierced resistance late in the session and closed just under the day's highs, buoyed by speculative short-covering and fund buying, floor sources said.

March options expiry on Friday kept dealings thin for most of the session, but activity accelerated once the March contract broke through key 10.60 cents, they added. The March contract settled 0.12 cent higher to 10.63, having ranged from 10.65 to 10.47 cents. The outer months closed 0.15 to 0.10 firmer. The May contract settled at a 0.05 cent premium to March compared with 0.02 cent on Monday's close.

NYMEX crude prices fell Tuesday morning, resuming a seasonal downtrend after snapping a four session streak of declines Monday. "We are establishing a lower trading range of $21.50 to $23.50, so we still have not seen the lows," said Jim Ritterbusch, trader with Sweeney Oil. At 1050 EST, March crude was off 10 cents a barrel at $22.36 while March heating oil was off 0.11 cent a gallon at 61.65 cents. Heat prices were repositioning themselves in tandem with distillate cash prices in the U.S. Gulf after both rose Monday on tighter cash supplies, dealers said.
